hero.title: The blades spin. You walk.
hero.lead: Blade of Ages: Çağların Kılıcı is a one-thumb action game in which outward-facing blades spin around your hero. Cut through waves of enemies and defeat bosses across {eras} ages and {realms} mythological realms.
hero.hint.pointer: Move the cursor and the hero follows. Stop, and the blades draw in and spin faster.
hero.hint.touch: Touch and drag. Lift your finger and the blades draw in and spin faster.
hero.canvas: Playable demo: blades spinning around the hero cut down Göbekli Tepe enemies coming from four directions; defeated monsters turn into gold.
how.title: One thumb, two orbits
how.lead: No extra buttons. The blades attack on their own; you choose where to stand and when to walk.
how.move.title: Walk
how.move.text: The blades spin in a wide orbit and clear your path as you move through the crowd.
how.stand.title: Stand
how.stand.text: The blades draw in close and spin faster, melting a tough enemy at short range.
how.parry.title: Parry
how.parry.text: Purple projectiles vanish when they hit a blade. Red area warnings have to be dodged.
journey.title: Journey through the Ages
journey.lead: {eras} ages, {realms} mythological realms, {maps} maps. Every realm has its own enemies, map rule, weapon and boss. When an age's realms are cleared, its guardian waits at the gate. Silik has faded the myths; your blades remember.
journey.erased: Silik has erased the memory of this age. It will return as the journey goes on.
era.era_1.blurb: Stone boars charge across the hill of standing stones; in the cedar forest of Uruk, roots lay traps.
era.era_2.blurb: Sandstorms narrow your sight, labyrinth walls shift, and lightning strikes the storm mountains.
era.era_3.blurb: Ice makes the fjords slippery, wind corridors on the steppe speed you up, and lights wander through the marsh.

fair.title: Fair play
fair.ads.title: No forced ads
fair.ads.text: An ad plays only when you choose to watch one, and it gives you a reward.
fair.myth.title: Respect for myths
fair.myth.text: You never fight the gods of living faiths. Bosses are the myths' own monsters and villains.
fair.gore.title: No gore
fair.gore.text: Defeated enemies crumble into their materials and turn into gold.
parents.title: For parents
parents.lead: What to know before your child plays.
parents.gore: No blood or gore: a defeated enemy breaks into the material it is made of and turns to gold.
parents.iap: The game is free, with optional in-app purchases. Diamonds, bought with real money, are used for things like refilling lives, looks and switching heroes.
parents.lives: Winning a campaign map in time costs no life; lives refill on their own over time.
parents.board: On the daily board players appear only under names the game suggests; there is no chat, and anyone can stay hidden.
parents.apple: You can manage purchases and play time with Apple's Ask to Buy and Screen Time settings.
parents.ask: Ask your child: which tale would you tell?
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.story.a: Blade of Ages: Çağların Kılıcı is an action game in which the world's tales live on the branches of a single tree, the Tree of Ages. Each branch is an age, each cluster of leaves a mythological realm: the standing stones of Göbeklitepe, the cedar forest of Sumer, the sands of Egypt, the labyrinth island of Greece, the storm mountains of the Hittites, the frozen fjords of the North and more. You are a Rememberer who tells these tales again; the blades spinning around you are your memory.
faq.when.q: When does Blade of Ages come out?
faq.when.a: Soon, on the App Store. The release date will appear on this page once it is set.
faq.devices.q: Which devices can I play on?
faq.price.a: It is free to download. The game has optional in-app purchases and no forced ads.
faq.langs.q: Which languages is it available in?
faq.myth.q: Are the myths in the game real?
faq.myth.a: The realms draw on real mythologies: Göbekli Tepe, the Epic of Gilgamesh, and Egyptian, Greek and Hittite myths. The bosses are monsters from these myths; the game's story and some characters are its own.

realm.story.title: In the game's tale
realm.story.gobeklitepe: The foxes, boars and scorpions carved in stone have fallen from the stones and forgotten what they were pictures of. On one stone there is a vulture. In the Storyteller's tale, Mother Vulture carried every carving to the sky and made it a star; now she has lost her way and circles above the stones. Defeated, she returns to the sky. The obsidian feathers she drops, the Obsidian Blades, are her keepsake. (Mother Vulture's tale is the game's own; no written myth survives from Göbeklitepe.)
realm.story.sumer: Humbaba, keeper of the Cedar Forest, is trapped in the darkest day of the epic: the day strangers entered his forest. Defeated, he refuses to return to that story and stays in his forest this time; the brightest of his seven radiances, the Bronze Sickle Sword, is his keepsake. Every telling changes a tale a little.
realm.story.misir: Apep, the serpent of chaos who attacks the sun's boat every night, has left the night; now the desert darkens with his breath. Defeated, he returns to the night and to his own battle: without him, morning would not be morning. The Khopesh, the colour of the sun, is the keepsake.
realm.story.yunan: Medusa is tired of being an obstacle in someone else's story. Defeated, she returns to her sisters; the statues in the arena step out of the stone, and her petrifying gaze becomes the protective face on shields. The Xiphos is the keepsake of the first hero freed from stone.
realm.story.hitit: Illuyanka has been torn from the tale told every spring at the Purulli festival; he still remembers the feast, but there is no table. Defeated, he returns to the earth to be told again each spring. The Iron Sword, forged from the mountain's iron, is the keepsake.
realm.story.iskandinav: Ravens search for Memory and steal everything that shines. Fenrir's binding has faded; the wolf no longer waits, it wanders. Defeated, you do not bind him again: he chooses to wait for his own time. The Spinning Axe is a dwarf's keepsake.

heroes.page.title: Heroes
heroes.page.lead: The {heroes} heroes of Blade of Ages: Çağların Kılıcı, each from a different myth and land. Every hero has their own weapon, play style and power.
hero.unknown: This hero's story is still being written.
hero.myth.kaya: About 11,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers raised T-shaped stones at Göbekli Tepe; Pillar 2 is carved with a bull, a fox and a crane.
hero.myth.nefertari: Nefertari, Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II ("Naptera" in Hittite tablets), wrote letters to Hattušili III and Puduhepa; she sent Puduhepa a gold necklace of twelve strands and fine clothes.
hero.myth.muwatalli: In the 13th century BC, Muwatalli II met the army of Ramesses II at Kadesh; the battle had no clear winner, and the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty was signed later, under Hattušili III.
hero.myth.antiope: Antiope is named as a sister of the Amazon queens Hippolyte and Melanippe; Themiscyra is placed on the banks of the Thermodon, today the Terme river.
hero.myth.aristos: Hoplites carried a large round shield, the aspis; Thucydides writes that in the phalanx each soldier sheltered behind the shield of the man to his right (Peloponnesian War 5.71).
hero.myth.nergal: "Adapa and the South Wind" is known from tablets found at Amarna (14th century BC) and in the library of Ashurbanipal; Adapa is the wise servant of Ea's temple at Eridu, and he does not eat the food of life he is offered.
hero.myth.sigrun: Sigrún appears in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I and II in the Poetic Edda; when she first meets Helgi, she leads nine Valkyries; the first poem tells how she guards ships in a storm from the sky (not verified: the stanza has not been read).
hero.myth.brigid: At the start of the Táin Bó Cúailnge, Fedelm, a poet-seer (banfhili) of Connacht, rides her chariot up to Queen Medb's army and foresees how the war will go.
hero.myth.jin: The jian is a straight, double-edged sword known in China for more than two thousand years, and it is traditionally called "the gentleman of weapons".
hero.myth.tomoe: No primary records of the Genpei War (1180–1185) mention Tomoe Gozen; the Heike Monogatari tells of her as an onna-musha who fought beside Minamoto no Yoshinaka.
hero.myth.itzel: In the Popol Vuh, Hunahpu strikes Vucub Caquix, who thought he was the sun, with a blowgun; in Maya tradition, the ceiba is the sacred tree that links the layers of the world.
hero.myth.tomris: Everything we know of Tomyris comes from Herodotus (Histories I.205–214); he describes the Massagetae as a steppe people living to the east, beyond the Araxes. Which river Herodotus meant by the Araxes is still debated.
hero.myth.rostam: In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (around 1010), the seven trials Rostam faces with Rakhsh are known as the "Haft Khan"; the Simurgh raises Rostam's father, Zal, in her nest.
hero.myth.arjun: In the Mahabharata, Arjuna is the third of the Pandava brothers and the owner of the bow Gandiva; he is remembered as Drona's star pupil. The bird's-eye scene is common in popular retellings; its place in the critical edition has not been verified.
hero.myth.vasilisa: "Vasilisa the Beautiful" appears in Afanasyev's collection Narodnye russkie skazki (1855–1863); white, red and black riders, standing for day, the sun and night, pass by Baba Yaga's house.
hero.myth.oya: Adeola is not a figure from myth. The Niger runs about 4,180 km across West Africa: it rises in Guinea, flows through Mali, Niger and Nigeria, and empties into the Gulf of Guinea.
hero.myth.tane: The mere is a short, flat club that Māori warriors used in close combat; the most prized were made of greenstone (pounamu), were often named, and were passed down as family heirlooms and signs of chiefly authority.
hero.myth.qori: The khipu was an Inca record-keeping system that stored numbers and information as knots tied in coloured cords; Qorikancha (Coricancha) is the Inca temple in Cusco.
hero.myth.lucius: A centurion was an officer in the Roman army who led a unit of about eighty men; in the testudo, shields were joined at the front and overhead to form a shell.
hero.myth.yushin: Kim Yu-sin (595–673) became a hwarang at fifteen and was the general who led Silla's unification of the Korean peninsula; his life is told in the Samguk Sagi.
hero.myth.unutus: Unutuş is taken from no myth: Unutuş belongs to the Tree of Ages, this game's own tale.
hero.bio.kaya: Kaya is a fictional hunter, inspired by the T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe and the hunter-gatherer communities who raised them; the animals carved on those stones are his neighbours. His blade carries the memory of the hands that carved these stones. When the Tree calls, he hears it first: its lowest branch is his hill, and if the stones fade, everything above them shakes.
hero.bio.nefertari: Nefertari is inspired by Nefertari, Great Royal Wife of Egypt. A letter sent in her name to the Hittite queen Puduhepa can still be read among the clay tablets of Hattusa. Her blade carries the memory of the messenger's road: a road that carried words, not swords. She answers the Tree because she knows that a peace made with words also fades when no one tells of it.
hero.bio.muwatalli: Muwatalli is inspired by Muwatalli II, the Hittite king who faced the Egyptian army at Kadesh with his chariots. In the game he is a king and a keeper of accounts: like the Hittite treaties that named the gods as witnesses, he records everything. His blade carries the memory of his chariot horses. He answers the Tree because if the mountains' tales fade, no one will know where lightning falls.
hero.bio.antiope: Antiope is inspired by the Amazon Antiope of Greek myth. The myths place the Amazons' city, Themiscyra, on the Black Sea coast beside the Thermodon river. In the old tales the Amazons are often an obstacle on another hero's path; this Antiope runs her own. Her blade carries the memory of her sisters. She answers the Tree so that no one else tells her story for her.
hero.bio.aristos: Aristos is a fictional hoplite, inspired by the foot soldiers of the ancient Greek cities and their great round shields. In the phalanx every shield also covers part of the man beside it; that is Aristos's whole philosophy. His blade carries the memory of the comrade who stood next to him in the line. He answers the Tree because one empty place in the line leaves every shield exposed.
hero.bio.nergal: Adapa is inspired by the Mesopotamian tale "Adapa and the South Wind". The wise mortal of Eridu breaks the wings of the wind that capsized his boat, is summoned to heaven and, following advice, unknowingly refuses the bread of life. His blade carries the memory of Eridu's hearth fires. He answers the Tree because one who will not live forever knows best what being told means.
hero.bio.sigrun: Sigrún is inspired by the valkyrie of the Helgi poems in the Poetic Edda; her name reads as "victory rune". In the poems she leads nine valkyries. The game's Sigrún carries no one from battle; she carries names, every name she is told. Her blade carries the memory of the ships she guarded in the storm. She answers the Tree because, in the north, names are fading.
hero.bio.brigid: Fedelm is inspired by the poet-prophetess of the Irish epic Táin Bó Cúailnge. At its start she stops an army with her chariot, a weaver's beam in hand, and tells the queen exactly what she sees, wanted or not. Her blade carries the memory of her years learning prophecy in Alba. She answers the Tree because when no one says what they see, tales fall silent.
hero.bio.jin: Master Jin is a fictional wandering master, inspired by the jian, China's straight double-edged sword, and by the wuxia tradition of wandering swordsmen trained in mountain temples. He knows how to meet an attack better than how to make one. His blade carries the memory of every student he met on the road. He answers the Tree because a wanderer notices fading roads before anyone else.
hero.bio.tomoe: Tomoe is inspired by Tomoe Gozen, the woman warrior of The Tale of the Heike. The tale remembers her as a fine archer, a fearless rider and a warrior worth a thousand, though whether she truly lived is still debated. Her blade carries the memory of the horses she rode in the Kiso mountains. She answers the Tree because someone has to remember the falling blossom.
hero.bio.itzel: Itzel is a fictional Maya hunter, inspired by the Twins of the Popol Vuh, who brought down Seven Macaw, the bird that called itself the sun, with a blowgun, and by the ceiba, the tree linking underworld, earth and sky in the Maya world. Her blade carries the memory of the Twins' patience. She answers the Tree because morning still has not come to her forest.
hero.bio.tomris: Tomris is inspired by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae in Herodotus's Histories. When King Cyrus of Persia wanted her land, Herodotus says, she told him to be content with his own kingdom and leave hers alone. The Massagetae rode the steppe beyond the river Herodotus calls the Araxes. Her blade carries the memory of the steppe's horses. She answers the Tree because the steppe writes its word on the wind.
hero.bio.rostam: Rostam is inspired by the great champion of Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. In the epic, Rostam and his horse Rakhsh pass through seven hard trials, the Haft Khan, and the giant bird Simurgh, who raised his father Zal in her nest, watches over the family. His blade carries the memory of Rakhsh, the horse that never left him alone on any road. He answers the Tree because this is the eighth trial.
hero.bio.arjun: Arjuna is inspired by the great archer of the Indian epic, the Mahabharata. As the story goes, his teacher Drona shows his students a wooden bird on a branch and asks what they see; Arjuna answers that he sees only the bird's eye. His blade carries the memory of Drona's lessons. He answers the Tree because even focus scatters when no one tells of it.
hero.bio.vasilisa: Vasilisa is inspired by "Vasilisa the Beautiful", an East Slavic tale collected by Alexander Afanasyev. Helped by a little doll her mother left her, Vasilisa goes deep into the forest to Baba Yaga's house, finishes every task and brings fire home. Her blade carries the memory of her mother's blessing on the doll. She answers the Tree because someone must always carry a lantern in the dark.
hero.bio.oya: Adeola is a fictional runner, inspired by the banks of the Niger, West Africa's great river, and by the stories of wind and water told there for generations; her name is Yoruba. Her twin blades carry the memory of the shore wind that taught her to run. She answers the Tree because a story the wind does not carry from shore to shore is stranded on the way.
hero.bio.tane: Tama is a fictional warrior, inspired by the mere, the short, flat club of the Māori tradition of Aotearoa (New Zealand). His name means "son" or "young man" in te reo Māori. His mere carries the memory of his ancestors, whose names he can recite one by one. He answers the Tree because when ancestors' names go untold, the road is forgotten.
hero.bio.qori: Qori is a fictional khipu reader, inspired by the khipu, the Andean system of keeping records with knotted coloured cords, and by Qorikancha, the gold-covered temple of Cusco; her name means "gold" in Quechua. Her blade carries the memory of the first cord she learned to read. She answers the Tree because every knot is a name, and a knot untied is a name lost.
hero.bio.lucius: Lucius is a fictional centurion, inspired by the centurions of the Roman legions and by the testudo, the formation in which soldiers locked their shields together like a tortoise's shell. His blade carries the memory of the eight comrades who shared his tent. He answers the Tree because when the line is not held the road is lost, and when the road is lost no one gets home.
hero.bio.yushin: Yushin is inspired by the Hwarang, the "flowering youth" of the Silla kingdom, and by General Kim Yu-sin, who became a hwarang at fifteen; but he is not Kim Yu-sin himself. The Hwarang travelled the mountains and learned poetry, music and the sword. His blade carries the memory of the flowering youths he walked with. He answers the Tree because only being told makes a one-season blossom last forever.
hero.bio.unutus: Unutuş is a traveller from the Broken Clock. Unutuş does not remember a name; with a broken clock, there is no growing older and no growing up. The hourglass crown and staff share the colour of the violet light deep in the Tree's roots. In the game Unutuş is unlocked through the story, and the biography fills in realm by realm. Who is Unutuş? That story is still being written.

meta.story.title: Story: the Tree of Ages and Silik · Blade of Ages: Çağların Kılıcı
meta.story.desc: The story of Blade of Ages: the Tree of Ages where tales live, Silik, the fading of untold tales, and the Rememberer who tells them again with spinning blades.
story.h1: Story: the Tree of Ages and Silik
story.opening: Once there was, and once there was not.
story.lead: Blade of Ages: Çağların Kılıcı is an action game in which the world's tales live on the branches of a single tree, the Tree of Ages. Each branch is an age, each cluster of leaves a mythological realm: the standing stones of Göbeklitepe, the cedar forest of Sumer, the sands of Egypt, the labyrinth island of Greece, the storm mountains of the Hittites, the frozen fjords of the North and more. You are a Rememberer who tells these tales again; the blades spinning around you are your memory.
story.tree.title: The Tree of Ages and the Spring of Memory
story.tree.text: The Storyteller says every people knows this tree by its own name. At its roots lies the Spring of Memory. Every tale that is told seeps into it as a single drop and feeds the tree.
story.silik.title: Silik
story.silik.text: A tale that is not told fades. For a while now the tree has been fading: the monsters of the tales have lost their way and spilled over their banks. Göbeklitepe's stone boars roam the Egyptian sands; harpies circle the Hittite peaks. People gave this fading a name: Silik.
story.blades.title: Rememberers and the Memory Blades
story.blades.text: The tree wakes those who can still tell the tales. The blades around you are the memories of other heroes. When you walk, the orbit widens, because memory wants to spread. When you stop, the blades gather and spin faster, because remembering asks you to stand still. Every creature you defeat returns to its own tale, and the light it leaves behind becomes gold. Forgotten, it turns to dust. Remembered, it turns to gold.
story.teller.title: The Storyteller
story.teller.text: A voice whose face you never see. It is the one who tells the tales of the ages.
story.ages.title: The ages
story.ages.text: At the gate of each age waits a guardian in which that age's tales have tangled together.
story.unutus.title: Unutuş
story.unutus.text: A traveller from the Broken Clock who does not know their own name. Their story is still being written.
story.myth.title: Inspired by myth, made for the game
story.myth.text: The Tree of Ages is this game's own tale. It is inspired by real myths and does not replace them. Gods of living faiths are never enemies; the bosses are the monsters and villains of the myths themselves. Each realm page explains the myth and where the game departs from it.
story.llms: The world's tales live on the branches of the Tree of Ages; a tale that is not told fades (people call this fading Silik) and its monsters spill into other realms. The player is a Rememberer whose orbiting blades are the memories of other heroes; defeated creatures return to their own tales and leave gold behind. The Tree of Ages is the game's own tale, inspired by real myths; gods of living faiths are never enemies.
